title: De motu vibratorio laminarum elasticarum, ubi plures novae vibrationum species hactenus non pertractatae evolvuntur

deep.reconstruction:
Context (E443, 1773): small transverse vibrations of an elastic lamina (Euler–Bernoulli beam). In Euler's time-scaling the equation is (d²y/dt²) = −b⁴(d⁴y/dx⁴), with b a constant of length combining stiffness and mass. The boundary conditions are those of a cantilever. The end x=0 is free, so y''=y'''=0. The end x=a is clamped, so y=y'=0.

Art. XI–XII (end of the previous page and the top of this one): Euler wants a 'general' solution, analogous to d'Alembert's for the string. He posits a power series in x whose coefficients are arbitrary functions of t, y = Σ c_n(t)(x/b)^n. Substituting gives the recursion c_{n+4} = −c_n''/((n+1)(n+2)(n+3)(n+4)). The four free functions P=c_0, Q=c_1, R=c_2, S=c_3 are, up to factorials, the Cauchy data y, y_x, y_xx, y_xxx on the line x=0. In modern form:
y = Σ_k (−1)^k (x/b)^{4k} [ P^{(2k)}/(4k)! + Q^{(2k)}(x/b)/(4k+1)! + 2R^{(2k)}(x/b)²/(4k+2)! + 6S^{(2k)}(x/b)³/(4k+3)! ].
Euler notes that each of the four series satisfies the PDE separately. This is a formal solution of the non-characteristic Cauchy problem with x as the evolution variable. The beam operator is Kowalevskian in x, not in t. Convergence requires P, Q, R, S to belong to a Gevrey-type class in t (|P^{(2k)}| growing no faster than roughly (4k)!/a^{4k}). Euler judges that it yields 'little gain' for the actual problem, because the boundary conditions at x=a cannot be imposed in closed form.

Art. XIII: he therefore settles for a particular integral, found by separation of variables:
y = cos(θ²t)·(A cos θx/b + B sin θx/b + C e^{θx/b} + D e^{−θx/b}).
He verifies it: −y_tt = θ⁴y and y_xxxx = (θ⁴/b⁴)y. He remarks that A, B, C, D are linear quantities (lengths). The frequency θ² is quadratic in the wavenumber θ/b, which is beam dispersion. He says he had already met this form in his first investigation, i.e. the 1744 elastic-curves work, the Additamentum to the Methodus inveniendi.

Art. XIV (continued on the next page): the four boundary conditions are imposed. They give A=C+D and B=C−D, and then the cantilever frequency equation cos Φ·cosh Φ = −1, where Φ = θa/b.
errors: Misprint in the original: in the second and third columns of the four series the time differentials are printed dt² but must be dt⁴ (with d⁴P etc.) and dt⁶ (with d⁶P etc.).
Sign misprint in the original: the last term of the S-series is printed '+ x¹⁵d⁶S/(4…15 b¹⁵dt⁶)'. The pattern requires '−'.

Notational inconsistency: on this page Qx, Rx², Sx³ appear without the powers of b (the previous page has Qx/b, Rx²/b², Sx³/b³), while the higher terms keep b^n. This is harmless, since it amounts to rescaling Q, R, S.

ideas.what: Power series in the space variable with four arbitrary functions of time as coefficients, giving a formal 'general' solution of the beam equation y_tt = −b⁴y_xxxx. Each of the four sub-series is itself a solution.
ideas.modern_name: Formal solution of the non-characteristic (sideways) Cauchy problem / Cauchy–Kovalevskaya-type expansion; analogue of the Holmgren–Tychonoff series for the heat equation (Gevrey-class data)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Analogous series for the heat equation: Fourier/Poisson era, with rigorous treatment by Holmgren (1908) and Tychonoff (1935); Gevrey (1913) for the function classes; Cauchy (1842) and Kovalevskaya (1875) for the general theorem
ideas.where_published: E443 itself, §§XI–XII. Discussed in Truesdell's Opera omnia II 11/2 history (Rational mechanics of flexible or elastic bodies) — unsure how much detail Truesdell gives on the series.

ideas.what: Separated standing-wave solution cos(θ²t)(A cos + B sin + C e^{+} + D e^{−})(θx/b), with frequency quadratic in the wavenumber.
ideas.modern_name: Euler–Bernoulli beam normal modes; flexural dispersion relation ω ∝ k²
ideas.where_published: Additamentum I 'De curvis elasticis' to the Methodus inveniendi (E65, 1744); E443

ideas.what: Application to clamped–free boundary conditions, leading to cos Φ cosh Φ = −1 (next page).

missed.claim: Euler drops the series route as 'of little profit', but it can be completed. With the free end at x=0, R=S=0 identically. The clamped end x=a then imposes two linear differential equations of infinite order on P(t) and Q(t), in operator form cos/cosh functions of a·(d/dt)^{1/2}/b. Exponential solutions of these reproduce the frequency equation cos Φ cosh Φ = −1, and their general solution is the modal superposition. This is the operational-calculus (Heaviside/Laplace-transform) route to the general solution that Euler said 'could not be expected'.
missed.quote: Interim tamen hinc parum lucri ad ipsam solutionem nostri problematis redundat.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historically it shows the transform/operator method for beam initial-boundary problems lying immediately behind Euler's own formulas. This is mainly of historiographic interest; the mathematics is well known today.

missed.claim: Euler implicitly treats the beam equation as an evolution equation in x rather than t: Cauchy data on x=0, four arbitrary time-functions. This is precisely the sideways/non-characteristic Cauchy problem whose convergence hinges on Gevrey regularity in t, as in Holmgren's and Tychonoff's heat-equation series. The link between this 1773 passage and the later Gevrey/Holmgren theory does not seem to be drawn in the historical literature (unsure).
missed.quote: quae quatuor series non solum coniunctim, sed etiam vnaquaeque seorsim aequationi nostrae differentiali quarti ordinis satisfaciunt
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It is an early instance of the formal sideways-Cauchy expansion for a higher-order dispersive PDE. That is relevant to histories of the Cauchy–Kovalevskaya theorem and of ill-posed (sideways) problems.

deep.surprise_reason: The modal solution and frequency equation are classical Euler material from 1744. The formal x-power-series 'general solution' with four arbitrary time functions is a genuinely interesting early sideways-Cauchy expansion, but it appears in a published, well-studied paper (likely noted by Truesdell), and Euler himself abandons it.
transcription_corrections: The dt² in the d⁴ and d⁶ terms is faithful to the printed original but mathematically should be dt⁴ and dt⁶.
The '+' before the x¹⁵d⁶S term is faithful to the print but should be '−'.
The S-row begins '+Sx³' (the image shows a smudged 'S ʸ³'); this is correct as transcribed.
